title: Test Stress and Anxiety are Not Inevitable
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that test stress and anxiety, while widespread — about 80% of his own students raise their hands when asked if they feel even 1% test anxiety — aren't an inevitable cost of testing but a solvable problem tied to how students prepare. He traces the mechanism through the Yerkes-Dodson performance curve into what he calls an "Anti-Belonging Doom Loop," where repeated anxious underperformance causes students to self-identify as "bad test-takers," which further damages their sense of Belonging. His proposed fix rests on a study led by Dr. Ayanna Thomas of Tufts University, which compared students who used retrieval practice against students who simply reviewed material, then artificially induced stress before a final test. Group B (retrieval practice) not only outperformed Group A overall, they showed no performance decline under stress at all, while Group A's performance dropped significantly. Stuart's takeaway is direct: frequent low-stakes retrieval practice, explained to students, is the practical antidote to test anxiety, not just a memory technique.
points: Stuart names a mechanism connecting test anxiety to long-term motivation: repeated anxious underperformance leads students to self-identify as "bad test-takers," which then damages the Belonging belief — an "Anti-Belonging Doom Loop."

The Ayanna Thomas/Tufts study he cites shows retrieval practice doesn't just raise scores generally — it specifically eliminates the performance decline that stress otherwise causes, a distinct and stronger claim than the usual retrieval-practice pitch.

His informal in-class poll (about 80% of students admitting at least 1% test anxiety) is used to establish scale before pivoting to the intervention, grounding the argument in his own classroom rather than only outside research.

The prescribed fix is specifically frequent, low-stakes retrieval practice explained to students — not test-taking strategy tips or relaxation techniques, which the piece implicitly treats as insufficient.
quotes: It's unpleasant and painful for students. When it becomes too much, it diminishes student performance (as all over-stressed situations do, per the Yerkes-Dodson Curve).
This self-identification as a bad test-taker produces anti-Belonging, which starts to trigger what I call an Anti-Belonging Doom Loop.

I asked my students to raise their hand if they feel at least 1% stressed or anxious during a test. My purpose here was to help normalize struggle, and sure enough, about 80% of hands went up in each class.
The good news, though, is that performance-inhibiting test stress and anxiety are solvable problems, provided that we give students the right kind of practice prior to tests.

Folks in Group B performed better than folks in Group A in both conditions. (This makes sense based on what we know about retrieval practice; it's such an important concept that I cover it at length in another of the principles — "Tests are the Best" — in my upcoming course.) But here's the cool part: folks in Group B saw no performance decline in Condition 2, whereas folks in Group A did significantly worse in the stressed condition.
In short: using retrieval practice as a study method not only improved test performance in general, it erased the performance declines you and I often see when test stress/anxiety are present.
What's the application? Teach your students retrieval practice! Use it in your class. Incorporate retrieval practice as often as you can.
